newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-ALLEN JOHNSON WANTS MORE THAN GOLD.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-ALLEN JOHNSON WANTS MORE THAN GOLD.

text.p: Despite Olympic and world championship gold medals and two marks just one-hundredth of a second outside the world record, Allen Johnson still feels slighted.
"I just get the impression from a lot of different people that they see me as a great hurdler only because they have to, because 12.92 speaks for itself," said Johnson.
Johnson emerged on the international stage in 1995 with victories in both the world indoor and outdoor high hurdles.
Last year he made no contest of the Olympic final and also twice clocked 12.92 seconds, 0.01 of a second outside Colin Jackson's 1983 world record.
Still he feels he has not received due recognition for his achievement and when asked about next month's world championships, replied: "I really want it bad".
"A lot of people are good for one year," Johnson said.
"I wanted to come back and back up that (the 1995 world title) last year at the Olympics, and I did that. This year I'm going to pay my dues for the third year in a row."
A 12.97 second time at Stuttgart made Johnson the season's only sub-13 second hurdler and served as a major confidence booster.
"I'm not going to shy away from saying I'm the best hurdler in the world right now," said Johnson. "I think I have shown that beyond a shadow of a doubt."
Yet, it upsets the 26-year-old Johnson that U.S. officials and coaches did not consider him for an early round of the championships' 4x100 metres relay team.

"I went to the coaches after the nationals and told them I wanted to run on the relay team, and they just laughed at me," he said. "Not that I expected I would get a chance to run, but I was hoping for more consideration.

"I was hoping they would give me at least that much respect, but I was wrong. Now I can understand why they keep losing the relay. The coaches, I really don't think they know what they are doing as far as putting the relay together."
European promoters also displeased Johnson by refusing to allow him to run 200 metre races this year, or relegating him to the "B" races.

"I'm not some duck off of the street," said Johnson, who has lifetime bests of 20.26 seconds in the 200 metres, 8.14 metres in long jump and 2.11 metres in the high jump. "I'm not going to put myself out there, if I am not prepared."
Johnson is preparing for Athens with special intensity.
"Ideally, I'd like to break the world record there, in front of the whole world," he says.

"I've said for a long time that I want to run 12.7, and I think I can this year. But do I think I can run 12.7 at the worlds? Probably not. I think I'll have to run 12.8 or 12.9 a few more times before I can go 12.7."
His stiffest competition at Athens may come from a man Johnson, in a way, helped gain entry into the meeting -- team mate Mark Crear, the Olympic silver medallist.

Crear finished fourth in the U.S. championships and normally would not have qualified for the worlds. But since Johnson is the defending world champion and entitled to a wild card entry, the U.S. were granted an extra competitor in the event and Crear was added.
"He's confident he should be the winner," said Johnson. "I can tell his attitude by just racing against him. His attitude is that he won't settle for anything less than first place. That's cool."
Johnson also sees Cuban Anier Garcia, Slovak Igor Kovac, German Olympic bronze medallist Florian Schwarthoff and Britan's Tony Jarrett as factors in the race.
Johnson's biggest challenger will have neither a uniform or a lane.
"I"m just trying to run against the clock," he said. "That's the greatest opponent you can ever have. You can never beat it."
